A 30B-class model must also read long Persian technical documents reliably, which I could not confirm. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. sections_md.risks:
- Access to tender documents: in 2015 Iran's government procurement data was rated 0% open, with no common tender platform found, not machine-readable and not openly licensed \[S, 2015.index.okfn.org/place/iran/procurement, read 25 Oct 2026; ten years old\]. The product works on documents the customer uploads, so it avoids needing a feed, but it cannot find tenders for the customer; whether issuers charge for or restrict document copies was not confirmed.
- Accuracy: a missed qualification condition or guarantee amount can disqualify a bid; I found no benchmark of open models on long Persian technical and legal documents, and tables and scans make extraction harder.
- Demand: tenders are won on price, relationships and qualification more than on document reading, and a firm may already have bid managers; the 216,667–300,000 toman a tender price is untested.
- Confidentiality: tender documents of some private and defence-related buyers are restricted; customers may refuse upload to a third party unless hosting is domestic.
- Sector concentration: qualified-company lists can be small, as in the oil ministry's list of 27 \[S, en.shana.ir/news/1593005, 10 Feb 2026, read 25 Oct 2026\], so some sectors have few potential customers.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

37.title: Knowledge-based company application and grant writer
37.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal on these assumptions. An application draft costs about 14,512 toman of GPU time (about $0.055) and gross margin is 97% \[D\], and the plans charge 560,000–900,000 toman per application against about 2.29M toman of writing time at the minimum wage \[D\]. Revenue per customer is about 2.55M toman a month ($9.59) against 471.3M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 187 paying customers on paper and 202 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (80 customers at month 12, 300 at month 24) breaks even in month 19, with a peak cash need of 5,157M toman (about $19,438), +211M a month at month 24 and cumulative cash still −4,401M; the conservative case (25 / 100) does not break even (−219M a month, cumulative cash −8,762M, a floor); the optimistic case (200 / 700) breaks even in month 13 with +1,145M at month 24. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 22, while cutting prices 30% or halving customers removes it. The customer base is a pool of about 7,882 knowledge-based companies counted in the Iranian year 1401 (2022–23) \[S\], of which about 2,000 lost their status in re-evaluations, so repeat applicants are fewer than the headline. I did not find the evaluation criteria, the fees or the programmes that fund applications, and the programme rules that drive demand change often. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. 38.title: E-commerce compliance checker (trust seal and consumer rules)
38.verdict_md: Verdict: weak on these assumptions. A site scan costs about 4,535 toman of GPU time (about $0.017) and gross margin is 87–93% \[D\], and the plans charge 31,250–62,500 toman per scan against about 429,000 toman of consultant time at the minimum wage \[D\]. But revenue per customer is only about 450,000 toman a month ($1.70) against 412.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 925 paying customers on paper and 1,505 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (500 customers at month 12, 2,000 at month 24) breaks even in month 21, with a peak cash need of 4,776M toman (about $18,002), +110M a month at month 24 and cumulative cash still −4,486M; the conservative case (150 / 600) does not break even (−256M a month, cumulative cash −7,815M); the optimistic case (1,200 / 5,000) breaks even in month 13 with +743M at month 24. Doubling the GPU price, cutting prices 30% or halving customers each remove break-even, and the base case needs 2,000 customers, about 3% of the 66,000 websites detected with the trust-symbol badge \[S\]. I found no rule that makes a scan mandatory, no price for a human compliance review, and no count of shops that actually fail the rules. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

sections_md.risks:
- Demand is not forced by a rule I could find: the E-Commerce Act sets duties on consumer information, advertising and personal data (Articles 59 and 67–77), but the one law summary read gave no penalty amounts \[S, mondaq.com e-commerce-law-and-cybersecurity-in-iran, 10 Mar 2023\], so shops may not pay unless a licence or renewal depends on it.
- Rule and trust-symbol conditions change: the trust symbol is issued through enamad.ir with the business licence under a regulation dated 19 Feb 2017 \[S, legalmondo.com/?p=4773, 5 Dec 2017\], and the current checklist was not read; a stale rule set produces wrong findings.
- Liability for wrong findings: a "compliant" result that proves wrong can be blamed on the tool; the service must be worded as guidance and not legal advice.
- Shops without websites: many micro-sellers trade on Instagram or messaging apps, which the crawler cannot scan the same way, so the pool of 66,000 sites overstates reach for social sellers (one search headline asks whether an Instagram page can get the symbol; title only).
- Substitutes: web agencies, the issuer's own review and free checklists; no price was found.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

Crawling and cleaning pages; checking pages against the rule set with the model and fixed rules; maintaining the rule set when regulations or the trust-symbol conditions change; generating replacement wording; monthly re-scans; sending alerts when a page changes.

Domestic GPU/cloud host; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); web agencies, shop builders and hosting firms as channels; a lawyer for periodic review of the rule set.

Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, an extra customer-success hire per 200 customers [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.

Crawling cost (bandwidth, headless browsers, blocked requests) is only the 15M toman a month of infrastructure [A] and was not measured.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 925 paying customers on the fixed-cost formula [D: 412.1M ÷ (450,000 × 0.99) = 925.0], and stepping through customer counts with the node and hires each needs gives 1,505 customers [D]. 39.title: Document classification and archive search for offices
39.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers but thin against compute cost and dependent on slow buyers. A four-page document costs about 1,827 toman of GPU time plus 222 toman of spot-checking and storage, 2,049 toman in all (about $0.0077) \[D\], and the plans charge 3,250–4,000 toman per document against about 14,302 toman of clerk time at the minimum wage \[D\]; gross margin is 55–63% \[D\], lower than a text-only service because Persian scan reading runs on a vision model. Revenue per customer is about 19.6M toman a month ($74) against 461.3M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 25 paying customers on paper and 33 with the nodes and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (40 customers at month 12, 150 at month 24) breaks even in month 11, with a peak cash need of 2,542M toman (about $9,583) and +1,161M a month at month 24; the conservative case (15 / 60) breaks even in month 17 with a peak cash need of 4,411M and +165M at month 24; the optimistic case (100 / 350) breaks even in month 6 with +3,186M. Doubling the GPU price removes break-even (−39M a month at month 24), while a 30% price cut delays it to month 16 and halving customers to month 15. Two cautions. First, my first draft of the prices (1,125–1,667 toman per document) gave negative gross margin on the two larger plans and every scenario lost money; I reset the prices to about 23–28% of the clerk's cost because compute cost per document requires it, so the result depends on buyers accepting that price, for which I found no competitor price. Second, municipalities and state bodies buy by procurement and may be limited to approved suppliers and domestic hosting, so the linear customer ramp is optimistic for those accounts. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

| Customer segments | (a) Law firms and legal departments with large paper and PDF archives — core. sections_md.risks:
- Procurement and approved suppliers: municipalities and state bodies may buy only through tenders or from certified office-automation suppliers; I found no rule either way, and sales cycles longer than the ramp assumed would delay break-even.
- Data residency and confidentiality: law-firm files and municipal papers are sensitive, so customers are likely to require domestic hosting and contractual secrecy \[A\]; no specific rule was read.
- Scan quality: stamps, handwriting, faxed pages and old typewritten letters degrade reading; the throughput proxy is an English-language benchmark and the only Persian result I have is a 98% word accuracy on a clean sentence set from an academic article cited in #21, not on archives.
- Compute dominates cost: nodes are 67% of base-case monthly cost at month 24, and backlog uploads arrive in bursts that raise the real number of nodes above the 30% average utilisation assumed.
- Price acceptance: the plans only work at about 3,250–4,000 toman per document, after a lower first draft failed on cost; a cheaper non-GPU OCR engine would undercut it, and I did not cost one.
- Substitutes: local office-automation and document-management vendors and scanning contractors; no price was found.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

- Real documents per customer, pages per document and the size of backlog loads.
- Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.

40.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal-to-viable on these assumptions, and decided by customer acquisition, not by compute. A document costs about 726 toman of GPU time (about $0.0027) and gross margin is 97–98% \[D\]; the plans charge 40,000–120,000 toman per document against about 286,046 toman of drafting time at the minimum wage \[D\]. Revenue per customer is about 531,000 toman a month ($2.00) against 507.1M toman of fixed cost, of which 130M is marketing, so break-even needs about 965 paying customers on paper and 1,176 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (1,000 customers at month 12, 4,000 at month 24) breaks even in month 13, with a peak cash need of 3,290M toman (about $12,400) and +1,116M a month at month 24; the conservative case (300 / 1,200) does not break even (−24M a month at month 24, cumulative cash −6,837M); the optimistic case (3,000 / 12,000) breaks even in month 7 with +4,325M. Doubling the GPU price, cutting prices 30% or halving customers each delay break-even (to months 15, 16 and 18) without removing it in the base case. The catch is that 80% of customers in the mix are one-time citizen buyers \[A\], so the base case needs about 3,200 new citizen purchases every month at month 24, and the 130M marketing line only works if each costs about 40,000 toman to win \[A\]. I found no count of complaints or petitions filed, no price for a drafting office or lawyer, and no rule on who may draft legal papers for others. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. sections_md.risks:
- Who may draft and file: I found no rule on whether a tool or a non-lawyer may draft petitions for others, or which filings require a lawyer; the judiciary's 2022 regulation covers electronic filing and does not settle this \[S, nourlaw.com\].
- Wrong legal basis: a petition that cites the wrong article or body can lose the user a case or a deadline, which creates complaints, refunds and liability; the service needs lawyer-checked templates and visible disclaimers.
- Acquisition cost: the base case needs about 3,200 new citizen buyers a month at month 24 at about 40,000 toman each \[A\]; free general chatbots can draft the same text, so a paid product must win on trust and form accuracy.
- Sensitive data: complaints contain names, disputes and evidence, and customers may refuse to upload them unless hosting is domestic; the E-Commerce Act's personal-data articles are summarised in #38 and no specific rule for legal papers was read.
- Seasonality and episodes: demand follows disputes and deadlines (tenancy renewals, fines, tax and insurance cases), so monthly counts will be lumpy.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

41.title: Clinic appointment bot with AI intake questions
41.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal-thin on these assumptions. A booking conversation costs about 423 toman (about $0.0016) including two SMS messages, and gross margin is 74–82% \[D\]; the plans charge 1,333–2,000 toman per booking against about 9,535 toman of receptionist time at the minimum wage \[D\], and about 1.6% of a general practitioner's visit tariff of 126,000 toman \[D, S below\]. Revenue per customer is only about 1.445M toman a month ($5.45) against 417.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 301 paying clinics on paper and 514 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (250 customers at month 12, 800 at month 24) breaks even in month 18, with a peak cash need of 4,231M toman (about $15,947) and only +64M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash −4,120M); the conservative case (100 / 300) does not break even (−185M a month, cumulative cash −7,002M); the optimistic case (700 / 2,500) breaks even in month 10 with +940M at month 24. Doubling the GPU price, cutting prices 30% or halving customers each remove break-even. Onboarding and support are the heavy cost: one customer-success hire per 60 clinics costs 42.6% of revenue per customer \[D\]. Booking marketplaces already list doctors, I found no price for them, and I found no rule on handling patient data. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

sections_md.canvas:
| Block | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Customer segments | (a) Doctors with private offices who answer booking calls through a secretary or not at all — core by count. (b) Clinics and polyclinics with a reception desk and several doctors — core by revenue. (c) Dental, physiotherapy and similar practices. Not targeted: public hospitals with state booking systems. Pool: about 100,000 doctors in Iran in a 2011 table \[S, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare\_in\_Iran, read 25 Oct 2026; the table gives no source\]; in Mashhad 2,915 physicians, about 45% of those registered with the council, had private offices in October 2013, 51.9% general practitioners \[S, jmmc.mums.ac.ir/article\_2284, read 25 Oct 2026\]. Applying 45% to 100,000 gives about 45,000 doctors with private offices \[D, rough: one city, 2013, and doctors have since emigrated or stopped practising; the Medical Council head said about 30,000 general practitioners were unwilling to practise over low fees, 9 Jan 2025 \[S, iranintl.com/en/202501093061, read 25 Oct 2026\]\]. |
| Value proposition | Patients message a Telegram, Bale or Eitaa bot, a web chat or a link on the clinic's page; the bot asks the intake questions the doctor needs (reason, duration, medicines, allergies, insurance), proposes free slots, books, sends the confirmation and reminder by SMS, and hands the doctor a one-paragraph summary before the visit; it does not give medical advice and routes red-flag answers to a human. The labour replaced is the secretary's phone and message time: 4 minutes per booking \[A\], about 9,535 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance \[D\]); the plans below charge 1,333–2,000 toman per booking, 14–21% of that \[D\]. For scale, the tariff for a general practitioner visit is 1.26 million rials (126,000 toman) and for a specialist 1.89 million rials (189,000 toman) \[S, iranintl.com/en/202501093061, 9 Jan 2025; the year the tariff was set is not stated\]. |
| Channels | Direct sales and field visits to clinics in the biggest cities; partnerships with clinic-software and medical-association vendors; referral from medical-supplier representatives; a free booking page for each doctor. |
| Customer relationships | Free pilot of 20 bookings \[A\]; setup call to load schedules and rules; weekly digest of no-shows and booked slots; one customer-success person per 60 customers \[A\] (onboarding is heavy). Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate. |
| Revenue streams | Monthly by number of bookings: Doctor office 600,000 toman for 300 bookings (about $2.26), Clinic 2,500,000 for 1,500 (about $9.42), Polyclinic 8,000,000 for 6,000 (about $30.16) \[A, no competitor price was found\]. Mix 70% / 25% / 5% \[A\] gives ARPU 1,445,000 toman a month (about $5.45) \[D\]. |
| Key resources | A scheduling engine with clinic rules; Persian intake question sets per specialty reviewed by a physician (clinical content, to be written); an 8B-class open instruction model with Persian capability; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month \[S\]) and SMS access through a domestic provider; 2 engineers, 1 field onboarding hire (40M gross \[A\]) and 1 customer-success hire. |
| Key activities | Loading doctors' schedules and rules; maintaining intake question sets; handling reschedules and cancellations; sending reminders; escalating red-flag answers; monitoring no-show and booking data for each clinic. |
| Key partners | Domestic GPU/cloud host; an SMS provider (domestic SMS is about 100–200 rials on the same network and 150–250 rials across networks \[S, sent.dm, 3 May 2025\]); payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee \[S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%\]); a physician adviser for intake questions; clinic-software vendors. |
| Cost structure | Fixed: team 209.1M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 1 field onboarding at 40M gross \[A\] × 1.23 \[S\]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 40M = 417.1M toman a month (about $1,572) \[D\]; one-time setup 120M \[A\] (intake sets and clinic pilots). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 60 toman per booking for SMS and handling \[A\], an extra customer-success hire per 60 customers \[A\], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity. |

42.title: Doctor dictation to structured visit notes
42.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but it rests on Persian medical speech recognition that I could not verify. A visit note costs about 856 toman (about $0.0032) including GPU time and audio storage, and gross margin is 76–82% \[D\]; the plans charge 3,000–4,000 toman per note against about 9,535 toman of typing time at the minimum wage \[D\], which understates a doctor's time. Revenue per customer is about 2.99M toman a month ($11.27) against 407.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 138 paying accounts on paper and 164 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (150 accounts at month 12, 600 at month 24) breaks even in month 13, with a peak cash need of 2,711M toman (about $10,219) and +691M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +1,643M); the conservative case (50 / 200) breaks even in month 22 with a peak cash need of 5,050M and +71M at month 24; the optimistic case (400 / 1,500) breaks even in month 7 with +2,189M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 18, cutting prices 30% to month 19 and halving customers to month 17. The decisive risk is accuracy: on the one public Persian ASR leaderboard I read, a general open model made 36–76% word errors and a fine-tuned Persian model 11–22% on general test sets, and I found no medical-vocabulary test or confirmed licence for that fine-tuned model. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

- Habit: doctors who already type quickly or use paper may not adopt dictation, and clinic noise degrades audio.

The doctor speaks the visit summary in Persian (with drug names, English terms and numbers); the tool transcribes it and fills a structured note: complaint, history, findings, diagnosis, prescription list, advice and follow-up, in the clinic's template, ready to paste into the record or print. The labour replaced is typing: 4 minutes per note [A], about 9,535 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance [D]), far below a doctor's own time value; the plans below charge 3,000–4,000 toman per note, 32–42% of that [D]. Foreign anchors: AI scribes list at $39–$119 per clinician per month for Freed, about $150 for Heidi's paid plan and about $200–$600 for Abridge, and AWS HealthScribe is $0.10 per audio minute [S, getfreed.ai/resources/cost-of-ai-scribes, dated 21 Jul 2026, read 25 Oct 2026; vendor-comparison page, not independently verified]; the Doctor plan below at about $4.52 a month is 3.8–11.6% of Freed's range [D], and a 3-minute note at the AWS rate is $0.30 against about $0.015 here [D].
Phone and web app with one-tap recording; clinic-software integrations; sales through medical societies and supplier representatives; a free trial to individual doctors who then bring their clinics.

Free first 20 notes [A]; custom note templates per specialty and per doctor; correction learning (the tool remembers drug lists and phrasing the doctor edits); one customer-success person per 60 accounts [A]. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate.

Monthly by number of notes: Doctor 1,200,000 toman for 300 notes (about $4.52), Clinic 5,000,000 for 1,500 across 5 doctors (about $18.85), Department 18,000,000 for 6,000 across 20 doctors (about $67.85) [A, no Iranian competitor price was found]. Mix 70% / 25% / 5% [A] gives ARPU 2,990,000 toman a month (about $11.27) [D].

A Persian speech-recognition model that handles medical terms, drug names and mixed Persian-English speech (an open Persian fine-tune such as gooya-v1.4 scored 11–22% word error on public test sets [S, navidved Open Persian ASR Leaderboard, 23 Oct 2026]; its licence was not confirmed); a note-structuring 8B-class instruction model; a medical term and drug list; a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month [S]); 2 engineers, 1 clinical language editor (40M gross [A]) and 1 customer-success hire.

Transcribing and structuring notes; building medical vocabulary and template sets; measuring word and field error rates with doctor-corrected samples; integrating with record or clinic software; keeping audio and notes secure.
Domestic GPU/cloud host; payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee [S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%]); a physician adviser; clinic-software vendors; medical societies as channels.

Fixed: team 209.1M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-success at 30M + 1 clinical editor at 40M gross [A] × 1.23 [S]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 30M = 407.1M toman a month (about $1,535) [D]; one-time setup 150M [A] (vocabulary, templates and doctor-reviewed test sets). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 20 toman per note for audio storage [A], an extra customer-success hire per 60 accounts [A], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity.

[S] Sindad GPU inference plan, listed 14 Sep 2026

[D] ASR 180 ÷ 30 = 6.00 s plus structuring (2,000 tokens in + 600 out [A]) ÷ (2,658.57 [S, A6000 vLLM benchmark, Llama-3.1-8B] × 0.8 [A]) = 1.22 s

Customer-success staffing at one hire per 60 accounts costs 615,000 toman a month per account [D: 36.9M ÷ 60], 21% of revenue per account. Speech recognition is 83% of GPU time per note [D: 6.00 ÷ 7.22], so the unmeasured 30× speed assumption drives the cost. Accuracy review by the doctor is not priced.

revenue.x: Break-even is about 138 paying accounts on the fixed-cost formula [D: 407.1M ÷ (2,990,000 × 0.99 − 708 × 20) = 138.2], and stepping through account counts with the node and hires each needs gives 164 accounts [D]. Accounts ramp linearly from month 4 to the month-12 figure, then to the month-24 figure; the 150M setup falls in month 1.

Account counts are [A]. At month 24 the base case is about 1,770 doctor users, 3.9% of the rough 45,000 private-office pool [D, above]; the optimistic case is about 4,425 users, 9.8% [D: 1,050 single doctors + 375 clinics × 5 + 75 departments × 20], and the conservative case about 590 users [D]. Cumulative cash at month 24 is −4,909M toman in the conservative case (payback beyond month 24, so the peak cash need of 5,050M came earlier), +1,643M in the base case and +16,531M in the optimistic case [D].

Churn is not in the cash rows (the customer path is fixed). Any Iranian price for dictation, transcription or clinic-software modules.
The number of doctors who type notes for every visit, and a current count of private-office doctors.
Rules on storing and processing patient voice and records.
Real speech-recognition speed on Persian clinic audio (30 times real time is an assumption derived from an English-pipeline benchmark).
Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.

43.title: X-ray and dental image triage assistant
43.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers in the base case, but thin in the conservative case and blocked by two things I could not verify: a Persian-population-validated image model and the medical-device rules for diagnostic software. A scan costs about 2,886 toman (about $0.0109) to analyse, including GPU time and a 3% specialist audit, and gross margin is 68–84% by plan \[D\]; the plans charge 7,500–15,000 toman per scan against about 19,070 toman of specialist reading time at the minimum wage \[D\], which understates a specialist's time. Revenue per account is about 5.55M toman a month ($20.92) against 510.5M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 118 paying accounts on paper and 135 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (120 accounts at month 12, 450 at month 24) breaks even in month 13, with a peak cash need of 3,921M toman (about $14,779) and +1,186M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +3,536M); the conservative case (40 / 150) breaks even in month 23 with a peak cash need of 6,983M and only +67M at month 24, and it has not paid back by month 24; the optimistic case (300 / 1,200) breaks even in month 8 with +3,815M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 14, cutting prices 30% to month 17 and halving customers to month 18. The decisive risks are clinical: I found no public accuracy figure for an image model on Iranian clinics' panoramic and chest films, and no Iranian rule on diagnostic AI, so the tool must be sold as a second reader whose findings a clinician confirms, and a licence for any open medical-image model is unconfirmed. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

sections_md.risks:
- Accuracy: I found no public sensitivity or false-alarm figure for an image model on Iranian clinics' films; missed lesions or false alarms would turn the tool into extra work, and the 3% audit rate would have to rise (at 10% the audit cost per scan is about 8,333 toman \[D: 83,333 × 10%\], which would cut the dental-office plan's gross margin to about 41% \[D\] and make the chain plan, at 7,500 toman a scan, loss-making).
- Image-model licence: open medical-image models are often research or non-commercial; none was confirmed, so the service may require training a model on licensed data, which the 600M setup does not cover.
- Device rules: diagnostic software may need registration as a medical device with the health ministry; I found no Iranian rule, so the product is described as a second reader and clinical liability stays with the clinician \[A\].
- Patient data: films are health data; clinics are likely to require domestic hosting and consent \[A\]; I found no specific rule.
- Adoption: dentists who read films quickly may see little value, and capture software from equipment vendors may not accept add-ons.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

44.title: Pharmacy stock and expiry forecasting with shortage-substitution hints
44.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal. The service is cheap to run, about 319 toman (about $0.0012) per daily order proposal with gross margin around 98% \[D\], so the result depends almost entirely on how many pharmacies pay and on a small team's fixed cost. Revenue per account is about 1.50M toman a month ($5.67) against 407.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 274 paying accounts on paper and 373 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (150 accounts at month 12, 600 at month 24) breaks even in month 18, with a peak cash need of 4,394M toman (about $16,561) and +227M a month at month 24, but cumulative cash is still −3,643M then, so it has not paid back; the conservative case (60 / 200) never breaks even in 24 months, with a peak cash need of 7,293M and −183M at month 24; the optimistic case (300 / 1,200) breaks even in month 13 with +825M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 22, while cutting prices 30% or halving customers removes break-even within 24 months. Account counts are heavy because chains count as one account but several branches, and the 8,500-pharmacy pool is an undated figure \[S\]. The tool forecasts demand and expiry from the pharmacy's own sales; it cannot forecast supply shortages, and I could not verify how pharmacy software, wholesaler lists or the national track-and-trace system would give it data. Substitution hints are suggestions for the pharmacist only. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

sections_md.risks:

45.title: Drug-interaction checker using Iranian brand names
45.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal, and it depends on a data source I could not confirm. A check costs about 251 toman (about $0.00095) including GPU time, and gross margin is 79–91% by plan \[D\]; the plans charge 1,000–2,500 toman per check against about 4,767 toman of a pharmacist's lookup time at the minimum wage \[D\]. Revenue per account is about 2.31M toman a month ($8.71) against 431.7M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 191 paying accounts on paper and 224 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (100 accounts at month 12, 400 at month 24) breaks even in month 17, with a peak cash need of 4,488M toman (about $16,919) and +290M a month at month 24, but cumulative cash is still −3,314M then; the conservative case (40 / 150) never breaks even in 24 months, with a peak cash need of 7,387M and −129M at month 24; the optimistic case (250 / 1,000) breaks even in month 12 with +1,240M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 21 and cutting prices 30% to month 23; halving customers removes it. The decisive gap is the interaction knowledge itself: the commercial references I found are priced and licensed abroad, and I did not find an open interaction dataset with a licence that allows resale, nor a mapping of Iranian brand names to ingredients. A wrong or missed interaction is a patient-safety matter, so the output must stay advisory. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

46.title: Lab-result explainer for patients
46.verdict_md: Verdict: viable-thin on the numbers, with a clinical-safety and demand question I could not resolve. A report costs about 1,052 toman (about $0.0040) to explain, including GPU time and a 2% physician review of critical values, and gross margin is 57–71% by plan \[D\]; the lab plans charge 2,000–3,000 toman per report against about 7,151 toman of staff time spent answering questions at the minimum wage \[D\]. Revenue per account is about 12.6M toman a month ($47.49) against 431.7M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 48 paying labs on paper and 52 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (40 labs at month 12, 150 at month 24) breaks even in month 14, with a peak cash need of 3,225M toman (about $12,157) and +813M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +1,528M); the conservative case (15 / 60) breaks even in month 22 with a peak cash need of 5,545M and +73M at month 24, not yet paid back; the optimistic case (100 / 400) breaks even in month 8 with +2,513M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 16, and cutting prices 30% or halving customers to month 19. The decisive gaps are demand and safety: I found no evidence that Iranian labs would pay to explain results, and the one 2026 industry article I opened says AI models are not benchmarked for lab results, with no strong clinical evidence on their reliability, and that software interpreting a diagnosis is generally treated as a medical device abroad. The service is therefore sold to labs as a plain-language explanation with a referral line, never as a diagnosis. Customer counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

47.title: Insurance claim pre-check
47.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but the demand evidence is thin: I found no count of Iranian clinics and no data on claim volumes. A claim costs about 3,353 toman (about $0.0126) to check, including GPU time on a 15-page file and a 2% specialist re-check, and gross margin is 54–77% by plan \[D\]; the plans charge 6,000–12,000 toman per claim against about 14,302 toman of insurance-liaison staff time at the minimum wage \[D\]. Revenue per account is about 22.3M toman a month ($84.13) against 431.7M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 25 paying accounts on paper and 25 with the node and hires counted \[D\]. The base case (60 accounts at month 12, 250 at month 24) breaks even in month 7, with a peak cash need of 1,836M toman (about $6,920) and +2,584M a month at month 24 (cumulative cash +17,754M); the conservative case (25 / 100) breaks even in month 12 with a peak cash need of 2,944M and +752M at month 24; the optimistic case (150 / 600) breaks even in month 6 with +6,598M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 11, cutting prices 30% to month 13 and halving customers to month 11. These results rest on three assumptions I could not source: that a hospital files about 6,000 claims a month, that a file takes 10 seconds of GPU time, and that hospitals will let a vendor read patient files. The real problem is documented: a meta-analysis found about 5% of claimed amounts denied in Iranian hospitals and documentation faults the most common cause, which is what a pre-check targets, but I found no evidence on how much of it software can prevent. Account counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

- Value proof: a hospital pays only if it recovers more than the plan costs; with 20% fewer denials \[A\] a 36M toman plan for 4,800 used claims needs an average claim above about 750,000 toman to pay back at the 5% denial rate \[D: 36M ÷ (4,800 × 5% × 20%)\]; I found no average claim value.

- Rule changes: insurer tariffs and requirements change often, and I found no machine-readable source; the rule base is a permanent cost.
- Insurers: insurers could build the same check or reject files from vendors, and I did not verify their rules on pre-submission tools.

48.title: Persian-food nutrition and fitness coach
48.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but whether Iranians will pay for it is unproven, and the marketing budget I assumed is probably too low. An interaction (a meal-photo analysis or a coach message) costs about 358 toman (about $0.00135) to serve, and gross margin is 79–87% by plan \[D\]; the plans charge 2,333–8,333 toman per interaction, against about 11,919 toman of dietitian time at the minimum wage for a 5-minute estimate \[D\]. Revenue per subscriber is about 640,000 toman a month ($2.41) against 732.45M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 1,291 paying subscribers on one GPU node \[D\]. The base case (3,000 subscribers at month 12, 12,000 at month 24) breaks even in month 7, with a peak cash need of 2,289M toman (about $8,629) and +5,595M a month at month 24; the conservative case (1,000 / 4,000) breaks even in month 14 with a peak cash need of 5,004M and +1,477M at month 24; the optimistic case (8,000 / 30,000) breaks even in month 5 with +14,786M. The 300M a month marketing budget implies only about 175,000 toman ($0.66) per new paying subscriber at month 24 \[D\], which I could not support from any source: with marketing at four times that level, base break-even moves to month 12 with a peak cash need of 7,567M and +4,695M at month 24, and the conservative case breaks even in month 20 with a peak cash need of 16,684M \[D\]. Open risks: I found no Iranian price for a diet app or a dietitian visit, the only Iranian food-composition table I found is listed as restricted access, and I could not verify that a 7B vision model recognises Iranian dishes or portions well enough to give calorie estimates. Subscriber counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

| Customer segments | (a) Adults who want to lose weight or manage a condition and eat Iranian home cooking, the core by count. (b) People with diabetes, hypertension or high cholesterol who want meal guidance between doctor visits, a sub-segment of (a). (c) Gym members and fitness-minded users who want a combined food and training plan. Not targeted: patients who need a clinical diet prescribed by a hospital dietitian. Pool: Iran had 92.6M people and 73.8M internet users (79.6%) in October 2025 (DataReportal Digital 2026, datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-iran, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S\]); 76.8% of the population was aged 15 or over (0–14 years 23.3%, 2024 estimate; Wikipedia Demographics of Iran, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S\]), about 71.1M \[D\]; 63.0% of Iranian adults had overweight or obesity in the STEPs 2021 survey (Frontiers in Endocrinology, 2022, frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2022.1043894/full, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S\]; the abstract and body text disagree on the sex split, 66% / 53% against 61.5% / 54.5%). That gives about 44.8M adults with overweight or obesity, and about 35.7M of them online if internet use is independent of weight \[D; 15+ population used where the survey covers adults, so approximate\]. The base case has 12,000 paying subscribers at month 24, 0.034% of that pool \[D\]. Karafs, an Iranian calorie-counter app founded in 2014, is listed with over 2 million registered users, but the Dealroom text is labelled as AI-generated (app.dealroom.co/companies/karafs, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S, unverified\]), so 12,000 subscribers would be 0.6% of that number \[D\]. |
| Value proposition | The user photographs a meal or types it in Persian (for example ghormeh sabzi with rice, or a kebab plate), and the coach estimates energy and macros, compares them with the user's daily target, and suggests the next meal and a short home or gym workout from local foods and habits. The labour replaced is a dietitian estimating one meal and replying: 5 minutes \[A\], about 11,919 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance \[D\]); the plans charge 2,333–8,333 toman per interaction, 20–70% of that \[D\]. That compares a minimum-wage person, not a real dietitian fee, which I could not find. The Premium plan at 2,500,000 toman is 141% of it because it includes a monthly dietitian review. |
| Channels | Cafe Bazaar and Myket listings (their commissions were not verified); Instagram and Telegram content on Iranian dishes with calories; partnerships with gyms and dietitian clinics; referral codes; a free tier of 5 interactions. |
| Customer relationships | Daily coach messages and weekly progress summaries; a monthly 10-minute dietitian review for Premium \[A\]; one customer-support person per 2,000 subscribers \[A\]; cancellation at any time because most competitors are freemium. Monthly plan billed in toman, indexed to the exchange rate. |
| Revenue streams | Monthly subscription by interaction quota: Basic 300,000 toman for 90 interactions (about $1.13), Plus 700,000 for 300 (about $2.64), Premium 2,500,000 for 300 plus a monthly dietitian review (about $9.42) \[A, no Iranian competitor price was found\]. Mix 60% / 30% / 10% \[A\] gives ARPU 640,000 toman a month (about $2.41) \[D\]. |
| Key resources | A Persian food and portion database (a licensed or self-built table: the Iranian Food Composition Table 2017 from the National Nutrition and Food Technology Research Institute is held in EuroFIR FoodEXplorer and listed as restricted access, with no licence stated, FAO INFOODS page, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S\]); a 7B-class vision-language model for meal photos (a non-text proxy); a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month \[S\]); 2 engineers, 1 customer-support hire and 2 dietitians at 45M gross each a month \[A\]. |
| Key activities | Building and checking Persian dish recipes and portions; testing photo estimates against weighed meals; writing safety rules (no crash diets, referral advice for medical conditions); running the monthly dietitian reviews; content and user acquisition. |
| Key partners | Domestic GPU/cloud host; app stores (Cafe Bazaar, Myket); payment gateway (Zarinpal and similar, worst-case 1% fee \[S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%\]); gyms and dietitians; the food-composition institute if a licence can be agreed. |
| Cost structure | Fixed: team 264.45M toman a month (2 engineers at 50M + 1 customer-support at 25M + 2 dietitians at 45M, gross \[A\] × 1.23 \[S\]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 300M = 732.45M toman a month (about $2,761) \[D\]; one-time setup 250M \[A\] (food database build and weighed-meal tests). Variable: payment and app-store fees 10% of revenue \[A\], 68.4 toman per interaction for the Premium dietitian review \[A\], an extra support hire per 2,000 subscribers \[A\], an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity. |

Holding 12,000 subscribers needs about 960 replacements a month \[D: 12,000 × 0.08\], plus 750 net additions a month in the second year \[D\], so about 1,710 new subscribers a month; 300M of marketing then buys each one for about 175,000 toman \[D\], which I could not check against any source.
sections_md.risks:
- Willingness to pay: I found no Iranian diet-app price, and Karafs is described as freemium with paid plans for advanced features (Dealroom text, AI-labelled \[S, unverified\]); if most users stay on a free tier the subscriber counts here do not hold.
- Estimate accuracy and harm: calorie and portion estimates from a photo are uncertain, and wrong advice to a person with diabetes or hypertension could cause harm; the Premium dietitian review and referral rules cost money and I could not verify what Iranian rules allow an automated service to say.
- Food data: the only Iranian food-composition table I found is listed as restricted access with no stated licence \[S\]; if it cannot be licensed, building a table of Iranian dishes and portions costs more than the 250M assumed.
- Model capability: a 7B vision model may confuse similar dishes and misjudge rice and oil quantities, and its Persian chat quality was not tested; a larger model would raise GPU cost, and the GPU-doubling row is the nearest proxy.
- Free substitutes: general chatbots and international apps can answer food questions at no charge to users who can reach them.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).
sections_md.unverified:
- Any Iranian price for a diet-app subscription or a dietitian visit (the Doctoreto dietitian pages, Cafe Bazaar lists and the Karafs App Store page are blocked or not fetchable, and the Persian app-review articles were titles only).
- Paying-user numbers or free-to-paid conversion for any Iranian diet app, and whether Karafs really has 2 million registered users.
- Accuracy of a 7B vision model on Iranian dishes and portions, and real GPU time per interaction (1.5 seconds is an assumption).
- Licence, size and access terms of the Iranian Food Composition Table.
- Rules on automated diet advice and on handling users' health data.
- Cafe Bazaar and Myket commissions, and the Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.
- The exact adult (18+) population; I used the 15+ share and an STEPs sex split that the source states inconsistently.

Check run: all \[D\] figures above were recomputed by running the model in code on 26 Oct 2026.

49.title: Therapist scheduling and session-note assistant
49.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal, and thin on demand evidence. A session note costs about 1,165 toman (about $0.0044) to produce, including 7.2 seconds of GPU time for a 3-minute voice dictation and a drafted note, and gross margin is 87–90% by plan \[D\]; the plans charge 8,000–10,000 toman per note against about 23,837 toman of a therapist's time at the minimum wage for a 10-minute note, which understates a therapist's real time \[D\]. Revenue per account is about 2.63M toman a month ($9.89) against 417.1M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 162 paying accounts on paper and 206 with the node and support hires counted \[D\]. The base case (90 accounts at month 12, 300 at month 24) breaks even in month 19, with a peak cash need of 4,369M toman (about $16,468) and +170M a month at month 24, but cumulative cash at month 24 is still −3,768M, so it has not paid back; the conservative case (30 / 100) does not break even, with a peak cash need of 7,548M and −197M at month 24; the optimistic case (200 / 600) breaks even in month 13 with +606M. Doubling the GPU price delays break-even to month 23, and cutting prices 30% or halving customers means no break-even within 24 months. The base case needs about 885 therapists, 18% of the roughly 5,000 licensed psychologists I found in one undated source \[D\]; I found no reliable count, no Iranian price for practice software, and no rule on storing session content. The product also depends on a Persian speech model that copes with therapists' vocabulary and on therapists being willing to dictate about clients to a cloud service, neither of which I could verify. Account counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

sections_md.risks:
- Confidentiality: session content is among the most sensitive data a client shares; many therapists may refuse cloud dictation, or the licensing body may restrict it, which would shrink the pool far below the 5,000 figure.
- Speech accuracy: Persian clinical and psychological vocabulary and mixed-language terms may push word error rates up; a 30 times speed assumption on a heavier model would raise GPU time, and the GPU-doubling row is the nearest proxy.
- Willingness to pay: therapists already use paper, spreadsheets or free messengers for bookings, and I found no Iranian price for practice software; the Solo plan costs about 1.3 sessions' income at the lowest fee I saw in a headline, but the headline year is unknown.
- Support load: at 23.4% of revenue per account, customer success is the largest scaling cost; if onboarding takes longer than assumed, break-even slips beyond month 19.
- Platform risk: reminders depend on SMS or messenger access, whose retail prices and rules I could not verify.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).
sections_md.unverified:

- Rules on recording or storing session content, and on holding client data outside the practice (the mental health law is described as still a draft in one directory guide, undated).
- Accuracy of Persian speech recognition on therapy vocabulary, the licence of the open Persian ASR model, and real GPU time per note (7.2 seconds is an assumption).
- Retail price of reminder messages (50 toman each is an assumption).
- Zarinpal fee and VAT, as in #1.

50.title: Hospital supply and bed-demand forecasting
50.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but the price and the data access behind them are assumptions I could not check. A daily forecast pack for one hospital costs about 339 toman (about $0.0013) to produce and the GPU is almost idle (the base case uses about 0.6% of one node at month 24 \[D\]); the cost is the team and the hospital integration work, not compute. Revenue per hospital is about 52.75M toman a month ($198.84) against 447.85M toman of fixed cost, so break-even needs about 9 paying hospitals \[D\]. The base case (15 hospitals at month 12, 60 at month 24) breaks even in month 9, with a peak cash need of 2,237M toman (about $8,433) and +2,353M a month at month 24; the conservative case (5 / 20) breaks even in month 15 with a peak cash need of 4,206M and +486M at month 24 (cumulative cash −1,732M, so not paid back); the optimistic case (40 / 150) breaks even in month 5 with +6,555M. Doubling the GPU price, cutting prices 30%, halving customers or doubling integration support keeps break-even between month 10 and 13. What decides it is outside the model: I found no price for hospital software in Iran or abroad (the foreign tools are all quote-based), no evidence that hospitals can export bed and stock data in a usable form, and no count of hospitals willing to buy; 60 hospitals is 5.4% of the 1,117 hospitals in one undated table. Persian narrative quality from an 8B model was not tested. Hospital counts are hypotheses \[A\]. Tags: \[S\] sourced, \[D\] derived and recomputed by code, \[A\] assumption.

sections_md.canvas:
| Block | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Customer segments | (a) Private hospitals and charity hospitals, core by willingness to buy. (b) Hospitals owned by social-security, military and corporate bodies. (c) Hospital groups and university hospital networks, core by revenue. Public hospitals under the universities of medical sciences are the biggest group by count but buy through university procurement \[A\]. Pool: one table lists 1,117 hospitals and 130,912 beds in Iran: 749 hospitals (90,003 beds) under the universities of medical sciences, 166 private (16,626 beds), 73 social-security (10,853), 32 military (2,190), 37 charity (4,198), 17 Revolutionary Guard (2,483), 9 oil-company (967) and 34 other (3,592), with 402,123 staff (BMC Health Services Research, table 2 of article 10.1186/s12913-021-07164-y, bmchealthservres.biomedcentral.com, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S\]; the table gives no year and the article is from 2021, so the data are older). Bed density was 1.6 per 1,000 people in 2017 (CIA World Factbook via IndexMundi, updated 18 Sep 2021, read 26 Oct 2026 \[S\]). At month 24 the base case has 60 hospitals or groups, 5.4% of 1,117 \[D\]; the conservative case has 20 (1.8%) and the optimistic case 150 (13.4%) \[D\]. |
| Value proposition | Each morning the hospital gets a 7-day forecast of admissions, discharges and bed occupancy by ward, a list of supplies and drugs likely to run short, and a short Persian narrative for the ward managers, built from the daily census and stock records the hospital already keeps. 51.title: Persian AI tutor for Konkur university-entrance preparation
51.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but the demand and the answer quality are unproven. The base case breaks even in month 11 and earns +2,337M toman a month (about $8,809) at month 24 with 10,000 paying students, about 1.0% of the 957,798 people registered for the 2025 Konkur \[S, D\]. The student counts are assumptions, no price for a Persian AI tutor was found, and a 30B-class model was not tested on Konkur mathematics and physics in Persian. Wrong worked solutions would end trust quickly. The unit price is about 1.4% to 2.4% of a private-tutor price in a press headline, which helps selling but also shows how much willingness to pay is assumed. The 10% channel fee is my assumption; at 30% (the 2017 Cafe Bazaar share) break-even moves to month 13.

| Customer segments | (a) Students preparing for Konkur and their parents, who pay, core by willingness to buy. (b) Konkur coaching institutes that resell seats to their classes. Pool: 957,798 candidates registered for the first round of the 2025 Konkur (Tehran Times, news/512513, 2 May 2025; the article says registered, not that all sat the exam \[S\]). A press headline puts a private Konkur tutor at 700,000 toman an hour (Aftab News, undated; page blocked, headline only \[S, headline\]) and another puts a Konkur teacher at 44,500 toman a minute (Tabnak, undated; page blocked, headline only \[S, headline\]); at 700,000 an hour, 15 minutes is 175,000 toman and the plans are 2.4%, 1.7% and 1.4% of it \[D\]. 52.title: Homework helper aligned to the school curriculum
52.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal-thin. The base case breaks even in month 15 and earns +895M toman a month (about $3,374) at month 24 with 8,000 paying families, but cumulative cash at month 24 is only +283M \[D\], and the conservative case (2,000 families) never breaks even and loses 198M a month. The family counts are assumptions; they are 0.05% of about 15 million public-school students in the base case \[D\]. Compute is cheap, so the risk is demand: the state's Shad platform reports 17 million activated students and is not shown to charge for homework help, and I found no price for any paid Persian homework helper. Curriculum rights, answer accuracy and rules on children's data were not verified.

sections_md.risks:
- Free competition: Shad is a state platform with 17 million activated students and free general chatbots are also open to students (their Persian quality was not tested here); paying for answers needs a clear edge in accuracy and in following the textbook.
- Answer accuracy on handwriting photos: I found no test of a 7B-class vision-language model on Persian handwritten homework; a wrong answer on a school question is easy for a parent to spot.
- Curriculum and content rights: textbook text and solutions belong to the state or its publishers, and I did not verify what may be used.
- Children's data and school rules: photos of children's homework are personal data, and school or ministry rules on such tools were not verified.
- Seasonality: revenue flat across months overstates summer months.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

53.title: Quiz and exam generator for teachers
53.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal-thin. The base case breaks even in month 15 and earns +534M toman a month (about $2,013) at month 24 with 6,000 paying accounts, but cumulative cash at month 24 is still −929M \[D\], and the conservative case (1,500 accounts) never breaks even. The account counts are assumptions; the base case is 0.8% of the 735,350 officially employed teachers \[S, D\]. Each of the three stress rows leaves month-24 profit near zero (+7M to +106M). No price for a Persian teacher tool was found, free English-language tools already exist, and the textbook content rights and Persian question quality were not verified.

54.title: Essay and short-answer grading assistant
54.verdict_md: Verdict: viable-thin on the numbers, with no demand evidence. The base case breaks even in month 14 with 15 paying accounts and earns +900M toman a month (about $3,392) at month 24 with 60 accounts, where an account is a department, faculty or institution \[D\]. The conservative case (15 accounts) never breaks even and loses 90M a month. All account counts are assumptions. The product sells to universities and schools, which buy slowly, and I found no Iranian price, no accuracy test of automated grading in Persian, and no evidence that universities accept machine-assisted grades.

sections_md.canvas:
| Block | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Customer segments | (a) University departments and faculties with large first-year courses and written exams, core by willingness to buy. (b) Private schools and tutoring institutes that grade short-answer homework. (c) Language centres \[A\]. Pool: about 3,375,000 university students in 2019 and 142 public universities (Iranian Science Center page, isc.ac, undated, read 27 Oct 2026 \[S\]); the page gives no private-university count, and the figure is older. The accounts here are departments or faculties, not students, so the base case of 60 accounts is not a share of 3,375,000 students \[D\]; with 142 public universities it is about 0.4 accounts per public university \[D\]. The counts (4 / 15 conservative, 15 / 60 base, 40 / 200 optimistic at month 12 / 24) are \[A\]. |
| Value proposition | The teacher uploads student answers (typed or photographed) and a rubric; the tool gives each answer a draft score with a short written feedback in Persian and flags answers where it is unsure, so the teacher only reviews flagged ones. The labour replaced is a grader marking one short essay: 6 minutes \[A\], about 14,302 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance \[D\]). The plans work out at 3,500, 3,000 and 2,500 toman a graded answer, 24.5%, 21.0% and 17.5% of that loaded labour cost \[D\]. Foreign anchor: Gradescope lists $1 to $3 per student, with institutional quotes in that range (toolsforhumans.ai, undated, read 27 Oct 2026 \[S\]; the page contradicts itself on which plan has AI grading), which is 265,295 to 795,885 toman per student \[D\]; the unit differs from a graded answer, so no direct comparison is made. No Iranian price was found. |
| Channels | Direct sales to department heads and deans; pilots on one course; university research-and-innovation offices; private-school owners; conference demos. |
| Customer relationships | A free pilot of 300 graded answers per account with a measured agreement against the teacher's own scores \[A\]; 1 support person per 40 accounts \[A\]; a monthly report on score agreement. Priced in toman and indexed to the exchange rate. |
| Revenue streams | Monthly subscription by volume: Department (1,000 answers) 3,500,000 toman (about $13.19), Faculty (6,000) 18,000,000 (about $67.85), Institution (40,000) 100,000,000 (about $376.95) \[A, no price was found\]. Mix 50% / 35% / 15% \[A\] gives ARPU 23,050,000 toman a month (about $86.88) \[D\]. Accounts use 70% of their quota \[A\]. The Doc 1 pricing note says per student; I model volume plans so they compare with other services. |
| Key resources | A 14B-class instruction model for scoring and feedback on a domestic GPU node (RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB, Sindad plan 150M toman a month \[S\]); handwriting and photo reading; 2 engineers at 50M each, 1 support person at 25M and 40M of an assessment adviser, gross \[A\]. |
| Key activities | Calibrating scoring against teacher scores per course, building rubric templates, measuring agreement, handling handwritten and photographed answers, supporting academics through pilots. |
| Key partners | Domestic GPU/cloud host; a payment gateway or bank transfer (worst-case 1% fee \[S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%\]); university course leaders who lend rubrics and sample scripts; an assessment adviser. |
| Cost structure | Fixed: team 202.95M toman a month ((50M + 50M + 25M + 40M) gross \[A\] × 1.23 \[S\]), GPU node 150M, other infrastructure 10M, accounting 8M, marketing 60M = 430.95M toman a month (about $1,624) \[D\]; one-time setup 300M \[A\] (about $1,131). Variable: gateway 1% of revenue, 20 toman per answer for storage and reports \[A\], GPU time per answer, an extra support person per 40 accounts, and an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity. |

sections_md.risks:
- Acceptance: universities may refuse machine-assisted scores for official grades, which would limit use to practice work and homework; I found no policy on this.
- Persian scoring accuracy: a 14B-class model was not tested on Persian essays, handwriting or rubrics; low agreement with teachers would end pilots.
- Slow public buying: public universities buy through procurement and budgets, so a 6-to-12-month cycle would delay the ramp.
- Price: no price was found at home and Gradescope's per-student price is a different unit; the plans may be wrong by a large factor either way.

55.title: English and IELTS speaking practice with feedback
55.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but the pool and the willingness to pay are not sourced. The base case breaks even in month 12 and earns +1,439M toman a month (about $5,424) at month 24 with 8,000 paying learners; the conservative case (2,000 learners) reaches break-even only in month 24 with +7M a month \[D\]. Learner counts are assumptions, because I found no count of IELTS candidates or English learners in Iran. The service uses English speech recognition, which is far better supported than Persian, but I tested no accuracy on Iranian-accented English, and whether learners can pay foreign competitors is not known.

sections_md.canvas:
| Block | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Customer segments | (a) Learners preparing for IELTS speaking for study or migration, core by willingness to buy. (b) Adults and students improving general English. | Value proposition | A learner speaks for 5 minutes on an IELTS-style question and gets a transcript, band-style scores for fluency, vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation, corrections, and a model answer; the intensive plan adds two full mock tests. The labour replaced is a tutor listening to and marking one 5-minute answer: 10 minutes \[A\], about 23,837 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance \[D\]). The plans work out at 10,000, 7,500 and 6,667 toman a session, 42.0%, 31.5% and 28.0% of that loaded labour cost \[D\]. Foreign anchors: Speak Premium $17.99 a month and Premium Plus $39.99 a month on the US App Store; ELSA Speak $19.99 a month on the App Store or $59.99 a quarter on its web page (speakshark.com, updated 28 Aug 2026 \[S\]); Speak Premium is about 4,772,657 toman \[D\], and the Plus plan here is 9.4% of it \[D\]. Whether those apps can be bought from Iran was not verified. |
| Channels | Telegram and Instagram channels for IELTS candidates, language institutes, IELTS teachers who recommend the tool, app-store billing (share unverified), and a free trial of 3 sessions. |
| Customer relationships | Self-service with a progress chart; 1 support person per 2,000 learners \[A\]; a monthly mock-score report; optional teacher review for institutes \[A\]. Priced in toman and indexed to the exchange rate. |

| Key partners | Domestic GPU/cloud host; app stores and a payment gateway (worst-case 1% gateway fee \[S, sources conflict: 0.05%–1%\]); IELTS teachers and institutes; examiner reviewers. |

Variable: 10% channel and payment fee \[A\], 50 toman per session for audio storage \[A\], GPU time per session, and an extra GPU node when load passes one node's capacity. |

56.title: Thesis and proposal writing assistant with Persian academic formatting
56.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, with an unsourced pool and an academic-integrity risk. The base case breaks even in month 7 and earns +3,509M toman a month (about $13,227) at month 24 with 6,000 active subscribers; the conservative case (1,500) breaks even in month 15 \[D\]. Subscriber counts are assumptions: I found no count of master's and PhD students in Iran, only an unsourced total of about 3.2 million students in 2023–24. The margin depends on a very low customer acquisition cost, so I added a stress with marketing ten times higher. Universities may treat ghost-written text as misconduct, and the tool must be framed as an editing, structuring and formatting aid. Persian university template rules were not verified.

sections_md.canvas:
| Block | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Customer segments | (a) Master's and PhD students writing a proposal or thesis, core by willingness to buy. (b) Final-year undergraduates with a project report. (c) University staff and journal authors preparing papers \[A\]. Pool: no count of postgraduate students was found; one site gives about 3.2 million students in 2023–24 across all levels, with no source cited (learningmole.com, read 27 Oct 2026 \[S\]), and the Iranian Science Center page gives about 3,375,000 in 2019 (isc.ac, undated \[S\]). The share that are postgraduates is not known, so no share of a pool is given. The base case of 6,000 active subscribers at month 24 is \[A\]. |
| Value proposition | The student pastes notes or an outline and gets a structured proposal or chapter draft in Persian, the university's heading and numbering rules, a table of contents, figure and table captions, Persian and English reference lists in the required style, and a consistent academic tone; a final check lists sections that do not follow the template. The labour replaced is an editor writing or formatting one section: 60 minutes \[A\], about 143,023 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance \[D\]). The plans work out at 11,667, 6,667 and 6,000 toman a task, 8.2%, 4.7% and 4.2% of that loaded labour cost \[D\]. A Persian article on typing cost (Maktabkhooneh) exists but its page is blocked, so no price per page was read. No Iranian price for AI thesis help was found. |
| Channels | Telegram and Instagram channels for graduate students, university associations, thesis typing and editing offices as resellers, search for Persian academic formatting queries, and a free 5-task trial. |

57.title: Plagiarism and AI-text detection for Persian
57.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, but demand is the weak point because a free national system already exists. The base case breaks even in month 5 and earns +4,884M toman a month (about $18,410) at month 24 with 3,000 paying accounts; the conservative case (900) breaks even in month 10 \[D\]. Account counts are assumptions: I found no count of theses, journal submissions or institutions that would pay. IranDoc runs a national plagiarism system that master's and PhD students must pass for proposals (PhD also for dissertations), and a university page calls a related tool free \[S\]; the product therefore has to sell pre-submission checking, AI-text detection and a report that explains each match, not the certificate itself. The reference corpus (theses, journal articles) is controlled by others and was not verified as licensable. AI-text detection in Persian has no accuracy figure I could source, and false accusations are a legal and reputational risk.

sections_md.risks:
- Free incumbent: the IranDoc national system is required for proposals and PhD dissertations; many students will use only that, and a university may reject a private report.
- Corpus access: the value of a similarity check depends on the corpus, and I did not verify that theses and journal texts can be licensed or crawled; building it is costed only as 250M setup and 30M a month.
- Accuracy and liability: false AI-text or plagiarism flags can harm a student; the product must present scores as evidence for a human reviewer, and Persian accuracy of AI-text detection was not verified.
- Evasion: paraphrasing tools and prompts reduce AI-text detection quality over time, so the classifier needs constant retraining.
- Willingness to pay: no price for a private Persian plagiarism check was found.
- Rial drift: toman prices need monthly indexing (the dollar rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\]).

58.title: Corporate training content generator
58.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, with the labour comparison probably overstated and the customer pool unsourced. The base case breaks even in month 5 and earns +6,640M toman a month (about $25,030) at month 24 with 1,200 paying accounts; the conservative case (300) breaks even in month 10 \[D\]. Account counts are assumptions: I found no count of Iranian firms with a training budget, and the only Iranian study found covers 20 organizations without hours or budget figures \[S\]. The price is anchored on the 49 to 79 development hours that Chapman Alliance reports for one finished hour of basic e-learning \[S\], but an AI draft replaces only the scripting and slide design part of that, not the whole, so the real saving per course-hour is unknown. Output quality in Persian, the need for a subject expert to check each course, and ownership of generated material are open questions.

59.title: Recorded-lecture summarizer and Q&A
59.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, with compute as the main cost and an unsourced customer pool. The base case breaks even in month 5 and earns +4,988M toman a month (about $18,802) at month 24 with 750 paying accounts on 16 GPU nodes; the conservative case (180 accounts) breaks even in month 9 \[D\]. Gross margin is 64% to 76% because speech recognition of long recordings is GPU-heavy, and doubling the GPU price cuts month-24 profit from +4,988M to +2,588M \[D\]. Account counts are assumptions: I found no count of Iranian online schools, only a headline that the Skyroom online-education market grew seven times in under a decade (zoomit.ir, title only, page blocked \[S\]). Persian speech recognition quality decides the product: on the open Persian leaderboard Whisper large-v3 scores 36% to 76% word error rate on the sets listed, while a Persian-tuned model scores 11% to 22% \[S\]; the licence of that model for commercial use was not checked.

| Value proposition | Upload or link a recorded lecture and get a transcript, chapter list, summary, key terms, practice questions and a chat box that answers student questions with timestamps. 60.title: Coding and Excel skills coach in Persian
60.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal. The base case breaks even in month 9 and earns +1,679M toman a month (about $6,329) at month 24 with 9,000 paying subscribers, which is 0.036% of the 24.98 million employed people in Iran \[S, SCI Q4 2024\]; the conservative case (2,400) breaks even in month 19 and has not repaid its cash need by month 24 (cumulative −3,373M) \[D\]. The price per subscriber is low (ARPU about $1.04), so the result depends on a large consumer base and cheap acquisition, and subscriber counts are assumptions. Free chatbots already answer coding and Excel questions, and I found no Iranian price for tutoring in these skills. The coach can only be sold if it does something free chat does not, such as run the learner's own spreadsheet or code safely and track a path.

61.title: Persian résumé parser and candidate ranking
61.verdict_md: Verdict: weak. The base case (450 paying accounts at month 24) breaks even only in month 17, earns just +224M toman a month (about $844) at month 24 and is still −2,555M cumulative \[D\]; the conservative case (150) never breaks even, and cutting customers by half or prices by 30% leaves month-24 profit at −59M or +35M \[D\]. Only the optimistic case (1,200 accounts) repays its cash need, and it needs about as many screened job posts as one large job site publishes. Revenue per account is small because each recruiter screens few posts a month, while fixed cost is about 372M a month. Account counts are assumptions. The one volume anchor is a dataset of about 365,000 JobVision job posts for 2022–2024 \[S\], about 10,100 a month \[D\]; the base case would screen about 38% of that monthly volume and the optimistic case about 102% \[D\], so the larger cases assume more posts than I could source. Fair-hiring law and privacy rules for candidate data were not verified.

62.title: Screening-interview bot and scheduler
62.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal and thin. The base case (360 paying accounts at month 24) breaks even in month 14, earns +443M toman a month (about $1,670) at month 24 and is still −156M cumulative; the conservative case (120) never breaks even, and halving customers leaves month-24 profit at +56M \[D\]. Only the optimistic case (900 accounts) clearly repays its cash need (+10,060M cumulative) \[D\]. Account counts are assumptions; they share the same unsourced pool of recruiters as the résumé screening service (#61) and I did not net out overlap. Foreign tools are priced for large employers: HireVue is estimated at about $35,000 a year for its entry plan and $50,000 to $100,000 or more for enterprise, and the vendor does not publish prices \[S\]; that suggests large Iranian employers are the only ones who could pay more than the plans modelled, and I found none to size. Persian voice recognition quality, candidate consent and legal limits on automated screening were not verified.

63.title: Job-description and ad generator
63.verdict_md: Verdict: marginal and thin, because free substitutes are plentiful. The base case (3,000 paying accounts at month 24) breaks even in month 13 and earns +443M toman a month (about $1,670) at month 24; the conservative case (900) never breaks even and ends at −4,158M cumulative, and halving customers leaves month-24 profit at +92M \[D\]. Revenue per account is about $1.05 a month, so the product needs thousands of paying accounts to cover even a lean team, and account counts are assumptions with no sourced pool. A search on 28 Oct 2026 returned many free AI job-description generators (builtin.com list, eklavvya.com, skima.ai \[S, titles only\]), and a general chatbot writes a job ad at no charge. The product would have to sell something beyond the text, such as Persian ad formats for Iranian job boards or salary-range guidance, and I found neither a price nor a size for that. This is best treated as a feature of a larger HR product (#61 to #70) rather than a standalone business.

64.title: Employee onboarding Q&A bot
64.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, with an unsourced pool of firms and a hard dependency on each client's documents. The base case (360 paying firms at month 24) breaks even in month 9 and earns +1,188M toman a month (about $4,478) at month 24; the conservative case (120 firms) breaks even in month 17 but has not repaid its cash need by month 24 (cumulative −2,124M) \[D\]. Firm counts are assumptions: I found no count of Iranian firms with 50 or more employees (the industrial-unit pages that turned up were robots-blocked, titles only \[S\]). The price is far below foreign tools: Leena AI is listed at $150 per user a year with a 1,000-seat minimum, and its vendor publishes no price (eesel.ai, edited 20 Aug 2026 \[S\]), whereas the plans here work out to about 15,940 toman per employee a month, about $0.72 a year \[D\]. Whether Iranian firms keep handbooks and procedures in a form a bot can read, and whether they will let a vendor host those documents, was not verified.

65.title: Shift and attendance scheduling optimizer
65.verdict_md: Verdict: viable on the numbers, with a pool of sites that I could not size and a value claim that rests on more than labour time. The base case (1,200 paying sites at month 24) breaks even in month 9 and earns +849M toman a month (about $3,200); the conservative case (300 sites) breaks even in month 22 and has not repaid its cash need by month 24 (cumulative −3,157M) \[D\]. Site counts are assumptions. The product is mainly a constraint solver on cheap CPU servers, so compute is small (51M a month in the model, an assumption) and the margin is above 97% \[D\]. The factory plan costs 139.8% of the one hour of manager time that a roster solve replaces \[D\], so for larger sites the price has to be justified by lower overtime and absence cost; I did not quantify that saving and the model does not claim it. Iranian rules the solver must encode (44-hour week, Friday rest, overtime at 140%, night work typically 135%) come from a secondary source dated April 2025 \[S\]; collective agreements and sector rules were not verified.

sections_md.canvas:
| Block | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Customer segments | (a) Shops, cafes and clinics with about 10 staff. (b) Mid-size sites such as restaurants, pharmacies and call centres with about 40 staff. (c) Factories and hospitals with about 150 staff on rotating shifts \[A\]. Pool: no count of Iranian sites with shift work was found; the plan sizes are \[A\]. 1,200 paying sites at month 24 is \[A\]. |
| Value proposition | The manager states rules and wishes in Persian or taps preferences; the tool builds a roster that respects the labour-law limits (44 hours a week, Friday rest, overtime at 140%, night work at 135% \[S, rivermate.com, updated 27 Apr 2025\]), staff leave and skills, shows the overtime and night-premium cost, and tracks attendance by phone. The labour replaced is a manager building one roster version: 60 minutes \[A\], 143,023 toman at 143,023 toman an hour (1405 minimum wage loaded with 23% employer insurance \[D\]). 66.title: Inflation-adjusted salary benchmarking and raise planner
66.verdict_md: Verdict: weak on the numbers, and the demand is real but unsized. The base case (300 paying firms at month 24) breaks even only in month 22 and is still 4,530M toman short in cumulative cash at month 24 (about $17,000); the conservative case (90 firms) never breaks even within 24 months (cumulative −7,848M) and the optimistic case (750 firms) breaks even in month 13 \[D\]. Firm counts are assumptions: I found no count of Iranian employers with enough staff to need a pay plan. Inflation is the reason the product could matter (68.1% in February 2026 per the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the minimum wage rose 60% from 20 March 2026 \[S, euronews.com, 17 Mar 2026\]), but the model charges 1,700,000 toman a month on average (about $6.41) against foreign tools that cost thousands of dollars a year \[S\], and the cost base is mostly people and one GPU node that the load fills to about 4% \[D\]. The product needs salary data that no Iranian source I could read publishes; the model assumes one data analyst (40M toman a month, gross) to build it from job ads and customer uploads, and the licence of any job-ad data was not verified. Usage is also seasonal around the new-year raise round, which the model treats as a flat 50% use rate \[A\].

sections_md.risks:
- Data supply: salary bands need data; job-ad salary ranges are often missing or vague, and the licence to reuse a job board's ads was not verified.
- Trust and confidentiality: owners must upload their pay lists to a third party; leaks would end the business, and customer uploads need anonymisation before they feed any benchmark.
- Seasonality: raise planning clusters around the new year (the 1405 minimum wage rise took effect on 20 March 2026 \[S\]), so monthly subscriptions may be cancelled after the round; the model uses a flat 50% use rate and 8% churn.
- Price anchor: foreign benchmark tools cost thousands of dollars a year; domestic prices of a few dollars a month were assumed and not tested.
- Inflation volatility: one source headline reports year-on-year inflation of 88.6% in June 2026 (page blocked, headline only \[S\]); rule and index updates must be monthly, and the exchange rate rose 30.6% from 24 Aug to 17 Oct 2026 \[D\].
- Compute assumption: token counts per run are guesses; the GPU is a fixed cost that the model loads to about 4%.
